RHINO-MAG: Recursive H-Field Inference based on Observed
Magnetic Flux under Dynamic Excitation
Hendrik Vater , Oliver Schweins , Lukas H ¨olsch , Wilhelm Kirchg ¨assner ,
Till Piepenbrock , and Oliver Wallscheid ,Senior Member, IEEE
Abstract—Driven by the MagNet Challenge 2025 (MC2), in-
creased research interest is directed towards modeling transient
magnetic fields within ferrite material. An accurate time-resolved
and temperature-aware H-field prediction is essential for optimiz-
ing magnetic components in applications with quasi-stationary
/ non-stationary excitation waveforms. Within the scope of this
investigation, a selection of model structures with varying degrees
of physically motivated structure are compared. Based on a
Pareto investigation, a rather black-box gated recurrent unit
(GRU) model structure with a graceful initialization setup is
found to offer the most attractive model size vs. model accuracy
trade-off, while the physics-inspired models performed worse.
For a GRU-based model with only325parameters, a sequence
relative error of8.02 %and a normalized energy relative error
of1.07 %averaged across five different materials are achieved
on unseen test data. With this excellent parameter efficiency, the
proposed model won the first place in the performance category
of the MC2.
Index Terms—power magnetics, machine learning, dynamic
system modeling
I. INTRODUCTION
Magnetics are usually one of the bulkier parts of modern
electronics and are responsible for considerable losses [1].
The continuously growing demand toward efficiency, minia-
turization, and sustainability places increasing emphasis on
optimized designs for magnetic components. The optimization,
in turn, requires accurate modeling and understanding of the
electromagnetic behavior and corresponding core losses of
the magnetic material. The modeling is difficult, because
the waveforms resulting from different inputs exhibit varying
degrees of hysteresis and saturation that are dependent on
the type of material, the core temperature, and the shape,
amplitude and frequency of the input waveform [1]–[4]. This,
paired with the lack of a satisfactory first-principle model for
the underlying processes, has led commonly utilized models
to be only accurate approximations for specific operation
conditions [4]. While physical first-principle models for the
micromagnetic material behavior exist, a transfer of the mi-
croscopic physical framework to macroscopic magnetic effects

A. Related work
For steady-state operation (e.g., in a DC-DC converter), the
usual process to estimate core losses is to employ specific
approximation equations, e.g., in the form of the Steinmetz
equation [5], [6], its various improvements [7]–[11], and more
recent developments such as the Stenglein method [3].
While these steady-state core loss models are valid ap-
proximations and very effective tools under the appropriate
conditions, it has been shown in the context of the MagNet
Challenge 2023 (MC1), that they can reach their limits when
faced with extensive and varied real-world data [12], [13]. In
MC1, this was addressed by encouraging the development of
data-driven material models that predict power losses based on
waveform, frequency, and temperature in ferrites in steady-
state operation [13]. Much progress towards general and
accurate models for core loss prediction in steady-state has
been made utilizing the tools from machine learning (ML) in
the context of the challenge (see, e.g., [4], [12]–[15]).
Beyond steady-state operation, there is a vast class of appli-
cations in which quasi-stationary or semi-arbitrary excitation
of the material is performed due to switched excitation wave-
forms, e.g., power factor correction (PFC) circuits, electric mo-
tor drives, and power amplifiers [16]. There are simple models
based on the Steinmetz equation utilizing the superposition of
the major and minor loop core losses for prediction of the
core losses in quasi-stationary operation of PFC circuits [1],
[17]. However, these concepts cannot easily be extended to
semi-arbitrary excitation conditions where the frequencies for
major and minor loops constantly change during operation.
For instance, for the electric drive, the rotation frequency may
change during operation, making the superposition inaccurate.
Additionally, superposition inherently assumes linearity which
is a simplifying assumption for the nonlinear material behav-
ior. Time-resolved modeling allows for more accurate consid-
eration of the nonlinearity. Furthermore, it allows modeling
of transients, and fully enables circuit simulation in the time
domain [4].
Classical approaches for predicting time-resolved hysteretic
material behavior include the Preisach [18] and Jiles-Atherton
(JA) [19] models, both of which are in essence phenomeno-
logical approximations, i.e., models that aim to mathematically
describe observed data trajectories and are inspired by physicalarXiv:2603.29745v1  [eess.SY]  31 Mar 2026

ideas but are not actually faithful to a complete physical
framework [20].
In practice, the JA model has been used, e.g., for the esti-
mation of core losses in electric machines with non-sinusoidal
excitations [21], [22] and for modeling of the material behavior
in finite element method (FEM) simulations [23]–[25]. Some
issues have been identified with the initial formulation of
the model. There is a risk of a non-physical negative dif-
ferential permeability [26] and, furthermore, non-closure of
minor loops and consequential drifting of the estimation is a
known problem when the excitation is not a closed loop [20].
Multiple extensions of the JA model have been proposed that
aim to improve the prediction quality including more precise
prediction of minor loops [27]–[30]. However, most of the
existing applications of the JA model are limited in the scope
of operating conditions. Some first approaches with adaptable
parameters have been proposed in order to allow more general
application (see, e.g., [26], [31]).
The Preisach model has been used for iron loss estimations
with different excitation waveforms (e.g., [32]–[34]) and also
has been compared to the JA model in prediction performance
for DC-biased hysteresis behavior [34]. The Preisach model
was found to be more accurate especially for increasing DC-
bias, but also required more computational effort [34]. In [35],
it was found that the proposed inverse Preisach was more
accurate and required less computational effort. However, they
utilized a closed form for the underlying Everett function,
reducing the flexibility of the Preisach model.
Ferrite materials are made up of an arbitrarily oriented and
shaped grain structure on the micrometer scale that heavily
dominates the macroscopic magnetic behavior. Physical mod-
els based on micromagnetic particle interactions such as the
Landau-Lifshitz-Gilbert equation (LLG) [36], [37] operate at
the nanometer scale. Transferring those to real-world mag-
netic material probes with heterogeneous, defective structures
remains an open question.
In summary, a first-principle model to explain magnetic
hysteresis that is reasonably applicable on a macroscopic scale
is missing [4]. Existing phenomenological, data-driven models
are only employed to different, small subproblems and never
really thoroughly compared on various operating conditions.
This makes it difficult to determine which model types are
most effective for varied and semi-arbitrary excitations.

C. Contribution
Considering the state of the art for modeling of magnetic
material behavior with transient excitation and the context of
MC2, the following contributions are made:
1) Design of a parameter-efficient gated recurrent unit
(GRU) model archetype for time-resolved modeling of
magnetic material behavior with an intuitive and effective
concept for warmup of the model’s hidden state.
2) Extensive comparison of a selection of model archetypes
for a variety of model sizes with respect to their pre-
diction accuracy in order to provide a Pareto front and,
therefore, a basis of comparison for further magnetic
transient modeling approaches.
3) Open-source release of the RHINO-MAG modeling
framework containing all of the presented modeling ap-
proaches online.2The implementation is made in JAX3
Python library for seamless utilization of accelerator
hardware (GPUs, TPUs) and just-in-time (JIT) compi-
lation.
With only325parameters and an average SRE score of
8.02 %and an average NERE score of1.07 %on unseen test
data, the proposed GRU with direct prediction (GRU-P) model
won the first place in the performance track in the MC2,
showing an excellent accuracy-per-parameter efficiency.

V. CONCLUSION
A variety of modeling structures for the prediction of time-
resolved magnetic material behavior were developed, imple-
mented, and compared in the scope of this work. It was found
that an almost purely data-driven model utilizing a single GRU
layer could provide excellent parameter efficiency in terms of
model size to model accuracy for small model sizes. As further
incorporation of physically motivated ideas could not improve
the performance of this model, it remains an open question
how to properly inject physically motivated structure into the
model and what kind of physical equations are actually helpful
for the macroscopic problem at hand.
To complement the presented work in the future, interesting
directions might be to perform a hyperparameter optimization
for the proposed model structures in order to ensure that
they perform as best as possible. Furthermore, the presented
Pareto investigations should be extended with the other models
that were submitted for MC2 to enable proper comparison
throughout different parameterizations. Additionally, it would
be interesting to consider transfer learning for the provided
model structures such that the model can be simply adaptedto a new material with only limited measurement data (cf. [4]
for a steady-state example of this).

structure.title: INTRODUCTION
structure.summary: This partial document introduces "RHINO-MAG," a novel approach for modeling transient magnetic fields in ferrite materials, driven by the MagNet Challenge 2025. The core problem addressed is the need for accurate, time-resolved, and temperature-aware H-field prediction in applications with dynamic excitation. The authors compare various model structures, finding that a black-box gated recurrent unit (GRU) model with a graceful initialization offers the best trade-off between model size and accuracy, outperforming physics-inspired models. This GRU-based model, with only 325 parameters, achieved excellent results on unseen test data, winning first place in the MagNet Challenge 2025's performance category. The document also discusses the limitations of traditional steady-state models like the Steinmetz equation for dynamic excitations and highlights the challenges in transferring microscopic physical models to macroscopic behavior. It contrasts these with classical phenomenological models like Preisach and Jiles-Atherton for time-resolved hysteretic behavior.

nodes.title: Related work
nodes.summary:
This document introduces RHINO-MAG, a novel approach for modeling transient magnetic fields in ferrite materials, motivated by the MagNet Challenge 2025 (MC2). The core problem addressed is the accurate time-resolved prediction of the H-field, crucial for optimizing magnetic components in applications with dynamic excitation.

The paper compares various model structures with differing degrees of physical motivation. A key finding is that a "black-box" Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) model, specifically a GRU with direct prediction (GRU-P), combined with a careful initialization strategy, offers the best trade-off between model size and accuracy. This GRU-P model, with only 325 parameters, achieved an impressive 8.02% sequence relative error (SRE) and 1.07% normalized energy relative error (NERE) on unseen test data, leading to its first-place win in the MC2 performance category.

The document details the challenges in modeling magnetic materials, including hysteresis, saturation, temperature dependence, and the lack of comprehensive first-principle models. It reviews existing approaches like the Steinmetz equation, Jiles-Atherton (JA) model, and Preisach model, highlighting their limitations, particularly for quasi-stationary and semi-arbitrary excitations.

The MagNet Challenge 2025 (MC2) is presented as a driving force for research in this area, focusing on time-resolved magnetic material behavior using a provided dataset of 15 ferrite materials. The dataset includes measurements under varying switching frequencies and temperatures, with a specific prediction task: reconstructing the H-field based on observed magnetic flux density (B) and other operational information.

The paper's contributions include:
1.  **Design of a parameter-efficient GRU model archetype (GRU-P)** for time-resolved magnetic material modeling, featuring an effective hidden state warmup mechanism.
2.  **Extensive comparison of various model archetypes** across different sizes to establish a Pareto front, providing a benchmark for future magnetic transient modeling.
3.  **Open-source release of the RHINO-MAG modeling framework**, encompassing all presented modeling approaches.

The general modeling setup involves estimating the H-field based on past H-field values, observed B-field, and core temperature. Feature engineering, including normalization and the derivation of finite-difference-based features (representing first and second derivatives of B), is employed to aid the model. A custom training cost function, adapted from RMS error, is used, which balances accurate H-field prediction with energy-related considerations. The document also outlines the parameter update process using mini-batches and backpropagation. Finally, it delves into the specifics of the GRU variants, particularly the GRU-P model and its unique warmup process.

nodes.title: GRU with direct prediction (GRU-P)
nodes.summary:
The document describes a machine learning model for predicting magnetic fields, focusing on its loss function, model architecture, training process, and various model types.

**Main Points Covered:**

*   **Loss Function:** The document details a normalized Root Mean Square Error (RMSE) loss function, denoted as L'RMSE, which is backpropagated to update model parameters. This loss function combines elements of SRE (Signal-to-Error Ratio) and NERE (Normalized Energy-related Error) metrics, incorporating quadratic tracking errors for accurate H prediction and pointwise errors weighted by changes in B for energy considerations. Normalization by the RMS value of the full sequence is used to prevent over-weighting of sequences with lower excitation frequencies.

*   **Model Structure Overview:** A general overview of the proposed model structure is presented, illustrating how raw input data is normalized, featurized, and split into two parts. The first part is used for "warmup" of the model's hidden state, and the second part, along with the warmed-up hidden state, is used for predicting normalized future field values, which are then denormalized.

*   **Parameter Updates:** The document outlines the training process, where material-specific models are trained over multiple epochs. Training data is split into subsequences and grouped into mini-batches. For each mini-batch, predictions are made, the training loss is evaluated, gradients are computed via backpropagation, and model parameters are updated.

*   **Model Types:** A significant portion of the document is dedicated to describing different model types investigated:
    *   **GRU Variants:**
        *   **GRU with direct prediction (GRU-P):** This variant uses a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) and directly predicts the magnetic field (H). It includes a "warmup" phase to initialize the hidden state and a prediction phase.
        *   **Magnetization GRU (GRU-M):** This variant explicitly predicts magnetization instead of H directly, aiming for a more physically grounded prediction. It explores different formulations for numerical stability.
        *   **GRU parameterizes linear model (GRU-L):** This variant uses the GRU's hidden state to predict the magnetic permeability of the material.
    *   **LSTM with direct prediction (LSTM-P):** This variant uses a Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) cell and directly predicts H, similar to GRU-P. The document notes potential differences in how the cell state propagation is affected by the warmup process compared to GRU.
    *   **JA Variants:** These models incorporate Jiles-Atherton (JA) formulas, which are commonly used for quasi-static hysteresis phenomena.
        *   **Basic (inverse) JA:** This describes the core JA model and how it's integrated with an ODE solver for magnetic field estimation. It also details how physical parameters are mapped to tunable parameters for optimization.
        *   The document mentions that the basic JA model has limitations in discerning different operating points and that subsequent variants address this.

nodes.title: LSTM with direct prediction (LSTM-P)
nodes.summary:
This partial document describes several variants of models used for predicting material behavior, focusing on hysteresis phenomena. It details:

*   **GRU variants:**
    *   **GRU-L (Linear):** A GRU parameterized linear model.
    *   **GRU-P (Direct Prediction):** A GRU that directly predicts the output.
*   **LSTM variants:**
    *   **LSTM-P (Direct Prediction):** An LSTM cell with a direct prediction mechanism, similar to GRU-P, but with noted uncertainties regarding cell state propagation during warmup.
*   **JA (Jiles-Atherton) variants:**
    *   **Basic (inverse) JA:** A model based on the Jiles-Atherton equations, which approximate the change in magnetization with respect to magnetic field changes. It includes parameters like saturation magnetization, anhysteretic magnetization, and coefficients related to domain interactions and hysteresis losses. The model uses an ODE solver for integration and a specific parameterization strategy to ensure physical parameter ranges.
    *   **GRU directly parameterizes JA (GRU-JADP):** A GRU that learns to provide the parameters for the JA model, allowing for adaptation to different operating points.
    *   **JA and residual GRU:** A model that combines the JA prediction with a GRU's residual correction. This variant is noted to have training instability and poorer performance.
    *   **Physics-informed neural network with JA regularization (PINN-JA):** This approach uses the JA model's prediction as a regularization term in the training loss of a GRU, aiming to improve convergence, robustness, and extrapolation accuracy by incorporating physical knowledge.
*   **Preisach model:**
    *   A differentiable version of the Preisach model, a phenomenological approximation of hysteresis. It involves a hysteron density function and a differentiable hysteron operator. The model's parameters, including the hysteron density vector, are optimized using gradient descent. The output function is adapted to include trainable weights and the GRU's hidden state. A preliminary comparison with a basic GRU-P is mentioned.

nodes.title: JA variants
nodes.summary:
The document describes several variations of a model that combines a Gated Recurrent Unit (GRU) with a Jointly Adaptive (JA) model, and also introduces a differentiable Preisach model.

The first variation, **GRU directly parameterizes JA (GRU-JADP)**, uses a GRU to generate the parameters for the JA model. The GRU's output is split, with the first five elements controlling the JA parameters and the rest potentially carrying additional information. This approach aims to learn how the JA parameters adapt to the current operational point.

The second variation, **JA and residual GRU**, attempts to combine the JA model's basic prediction with a GRU correction. This is achieved by summing the outputs of both models. However, this model is noted to have issues, including unstable training, a need for double precision, increased training time, and worse performance compared to setups without the JA, suggesting the JA information might be negligible or detrimental.

The third variation, **Physics-informed neural network with JA regularization**, integrates the JA model's prediction into the training loss of a GRU. This is inspired by Physics-Informed Neural Networks (PINNs), where physical equations are incorporated to improve convergence, robustness, and extrapolation accuracy. The training loss is a combination of a standard RMSE loss and a regularization term based on the difference between the JA prediction and the actual change in the state. The document suggests that in this setup, the JA might not be effectively utilized due to its poor prediction performance.

Finally, the document introduces the **Preisach model**, a phenomenological approximation of hysteresis in magnetic materials. A differentiable version is implemented, allowing optimization via gradient descent. The model involves a hysteron density function and a hysteron operator. The prediction function is a sum of contributions from discretized hysterons. The output function is further adapted with trainable weights. A preliminary comparison between this adapted Preisach model and a basic GRU-P is mentioned, with both trained and evaluated on specific material data.

nodes.title: Vector field GRU (GRU-V)
nodes.summary:
The partial document describes a "Vector field GRU (GRU-V)" model, which uses a 2D grid of 2D vectors to approximate a discretized vector field of magnetization. It details the prediction function for this model, including a modified version to address numerical issues. The document also discusses the initial intention to use the LLG as a regularization term, which was later abandoned due to infeasibility. The GRU-V is presented as a distinct prediction function from GRU-P and faces challenges with warm-up due to the complexity of its hidden state interpretation.

The document then transitions to a model overview, mentioning a qualitative comparison table (Tab. II) of different model types, some of which were excluded from empirical evaluation due to poor performance or computational infeasibility. The model size is presented as a rough guideline for typical application ranges.

The results section focuses on the evaluation of proposed models on a subset of materials from the MagNetX database. It details the model selection process for submission to MC2, emphasizing a true training-test split and the investigation of the trade-off between model size (number of hidden units) and accuracy (measured by SRE and NERE scores). The selection of submitted models was based on a good trade-off between size and accuracy, highlighting the scalability of the GRU-based approach.

Finally, an extended Pareto investigation is described, performed after the availability of the test dataset, to evaluate the previous model selection and compare proposed model structures with other MC2 submissions. This investigation visualizes the performance of individual models and the median error of model types against model sizes, also including the performance of models submitted by other teams.

structure.title: CONCLUSION

*   **Accuracy vs. Model Size Tradeoff:** The document highlights the trade-off between model accuracy and its size (number of parameters), particularly for GRU-P models. This is crucial for applications like FEM simulations where computational effort scales with model size.
*   **Data-Driven Models:** It emphasizes the effectiveness of purely data-driven models, specifically a single GRU layer, for achieving good parameter efficiency, especially at smaller model sizes.

*   **Future Research Directions:** Potential future work includes hyperparameter optimization for proposed models, extending Pareto investigations to other submitted models for comprehensive comparison, and exploring transfer learning for adapting models to new materials with limited data.
